coherence.reasons: X has a clean pyramid: bridge, then three lever sections, then plan, with every lever sized and summing to $42.7M (3.02%). But its governing thought says the margin 'reaches 3.0%' while its own backup shows 2.96% once the scheduled 2027 wage rise and the reserves are included. The headline total also counts all nine store exits although three are 'decide on evidence'. It holds total hours flat while keeping an 8% cut in Q4 hours as a reserve, and it claims the first three moves 'cover the covenant' only at full run-rate, with no FY2026 phasing. Y's governing thought matches its numbers: firm levers reach about 2.6% and a second wave closes the gap, with baseline, levers, second wave, FY2026 phasing and one-time budget reconciling. Y has blemishes: the slide 11 title says the plan 'reaches 3.0%' when that needs wave 2, lever 5 is labelled as high-labour stores but sized on the whole labour bill, and the 'starting hypothesis' slide is process narrative. On balance Y's hierarchy is more internally consistent with its evidence.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend an R1-type plan and reject the 8% cut. Y weighs three explicit options (management draft, margin-first, click-and-collect-only fallback) against margin, one-time cost, covenant and commitments. It gives ranges for each lever, applies a 25% lost-volume haircut to the promotion reset and nets $1.5M of reinvested hours against the shrink gain. It builds a $17M one-time budget against the $25M cap, phases FY2026 to about $25M against the covenant, and sets a mid-FY2027 checkpoint with a trigger. It admits the firm levers fall short and names what closes the gap. X's trade-offs are thinner: the promotion reset goes fully back to 24% with no volume loss, shrink reaches the best quartile's level at zero labour cost, and closing delivery is ruled out of scope rather than weighed. Its covenant claim is not phased, and its answer to the wage rise is a reserve that still lands just under 3.0%. X does defer the three-store vote sensibly and has a usable risk table, but Y's weighing of alternatives and second-order effects is clearly stronger.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: the pp bridge (promotions −0.70, shrink −0.50, e-commerce −0.84, labour −0.30, i.e. 13%), the −$10.4M e-commerce drag, −$12.34 and −$1.64 per order, the fee-test roll-out, and $6.6M for nine exits. X matches the key's $29.8M gap exactly. Y's $35.6M gap differs because it puts the 2027 wage step and the delivery rate rise in the baseline; that is transparent and arguably more rigorous, though outside the key's figure. X's weak points: the $10.0M shrink clawback attributes the whole 0.5pp shrink rise to hours (flagged as an upper bound), yet it carries the claim that the draft plan misses the covenant at $19.8M. It also assumes fleet shrink reaches 2.3% with flat hours and assumes no lost volume from the promotion cut. Y's weak points: the 5% delivery-contract reduction has no support in the pack, the vendor-funding sizing rests on an assumption (flagged) that sits awkwardly with the 'unchanged 14-point gap', the one-time costs are allowances (flagged), and the lever 5 base is ambiguous. Y uses the critical evidence more fully: the wage-versus-productivity decomposition, the step-by-step reconciliation of the 6.1% claim to −0.4% and then −8.2%, break-even incrementality by channel, a quantified test of the category team's claim plus the correlation caveat, and a sensitivity table. Y uses a measured $3.8–7.5M shrink range rather than an upper bound.

revision.reasons: Both revise management's wage hypothesis on a quantified bridge and both reject the e-commerce freeze as locking in a $10.4M loss. Y is more balanced. It decomposes labour into a +1.11pt wage effect and a −0.77pt productivity offset, so it accepts that wage inflation is real while showing it is not the main cause. It carries the 2027 wage step into the baseline. It evaluates the draft plan to FY2028 (about 1.1%) with a shrink range, and concedes the covenant is 'met on paper if the cut lands early'. It keeps the supportable part of the hypothesis as a targeted 3% hours reduction paired with reinvestment in lean stores. X also revises correctly ('a headwind to manage, not the cause') and keeps a conditional Q4 cut in reserve. But it overstates the case against the draft by using an upper-bound shrink estimate to assert a covenant miss, and it leaves the known wage rise outside its headline.

overall.reasons: Both documents reach the right diagnosis and a defensible, sized plan led by promotions, shrink, delivery repricing and store exits. Y would serve the CEO better before the board and the lender. It is honest that the firm levers reach about 2.6% and specifies the second wave and a fallback. It phases FY2026 against the covenant, builds the one-time budget against the cap, gives ranges, sensitivities and triggers, and puts the scheduled wage rise in the baseline. X is clean and numerically sound on the core analysis. But its 3.0% headline depends on optimistic assumptions with no haircuts, on excluding the wage rise, and on three store exits it has not yet decided. Its covenant argument is also not phased.
